Summary:
This article (300-words abstract) addresses moral preference aggregation for AI-driven kidney-exchange allocation. The authors propose learning a distribution over heterogeneous human moral preferences from survey dilemmas and dynamically sampling patient weights during the matching optimisation. Simulated evaluation shows higher average preference-rank of matched patients, indicating better alignment with community values.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[86]

Inference strategy justification:
The abstract contains all reasoning steps but compresses details. Moderate inference (confidence level 2) was applied only where implementation specifics (e.g., Bayesian inference) are implicit. All other edges rely on explicit statements (confidence 3).

Extraction completeness explanation:
Every explicit causal-interventional element (risk → conflicting preferences → modelling insight → dynamic weighting approach → implementation technique → empirical result → proposed deployment) has been captured. Nodes are named to merge cleanly with other sources (problem-specific but canonical wording). No isolated nodes remain.

Key limitations:
• The abstract lacks full methodology, so implementation detail is summarised.  
• Validation evidence is based on a single study; confidence remains medium.  
• Lifecycle/maturity ratings are approximate because deployment status is not stated.

Instruction-set improvement suggestion:
Provide guidance for choosing lifecycle stage and maturity when a paper reports only simulation studies (pre-deployment). Clarify whether multiple closely related implementation details should be merged or kept separate.
